As "vibecoding" becomes increasingly popular, the number of new apps listed on the App Store surged in the first half of 2026, doubling, though downloads only grew by 2%. Details below.

New listings surge, but downloads fail to keep up

A report published today by The New York Times, citing Sensor Tower data, indicates that the number of new apps listed on the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, while downloads increased by only 2%.

The New York Times report also mentioned two developers who have been releasing "vibecoded" apps on the App Store — Marco Pérez, who plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to develop apps full-time, and David Svensson, who has launched 11 niche apps in the past five months, viewing "vibecoding" as a hobby rather than a business opportunity.

Below is the report content:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never developed a mobile app before. He spent five weeks over the winter exploring "vibecoding" AI tools to create a prototype, then took two weeks to prepare the app for release on the App Store. The app, called InfoDrizzle, performed reasonably well, recording 1,300 downloads to date and earning around US$500. Pérez's next app performed even better. In May, he launched Stampa in about a week — a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps. Stampa has recorded 20,000 downloads and earned around US$3,000.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian issued a statement to The New York Times in response to another impact of this surge in submissions — the previously reported strain on the App Store review process.

Ajemian said: "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple is "delighted to see a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and launch apps faster."

He also stated that regardless of whether apps are developed through "vibecoding," "all apps must meet the same strict standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have come to trust."
